translation: Miho and Satsuki, by virtue of their frequent meetings, sport strikingly similar expressions and ways of talking.
In particular, their manner of eating sweets is so alike: they both break cookies into small pieces with their manicured hands before carrying them to their mouths.
I try to remember if it's always been this way, but my memory is hazy.
The little quirks and gestures from the last time we met might have already slipped away somewhere.
Miho is now married and she bought a used single-family home in her hometown, where friends often gather.
Sometimes she dreads going to her part-time job the next day, but it's her only connection to the world outside the convenience store.
It is also a valuable opportunity to interact with other 'normal' women in their thirties, so she tries to accept Miho's invitations whenever possible.
Today as well, Miho and I were having tea with Yukari who has young children and Satsuki who is married but doesn't have kids yet at Miho's house where we all brought cakes.
That was the first time I felt I had become a part of the world.
It was as if I had been born anew.
On that day, I emerged as a functioning component of society.
For the two weeks leading up to the opening, endless practice continued where pairs or groups would serve imaginary customers and company employees.
Smiling, making eye contact, and bowing properly; putting menstruating products in paper bags;
separating hot items from cold ones;
sanitizing hands with alcohol when asked for fast food.

To familiarize ourselves with handling money, real cash was put in the till, though everything was stamped "training" on the receipts while dealing with co-workers dressed in the same uniforms gave off an air of make-believe shopping.
My younger sister, two years my junior, was unlike me—a normal child.
Yet she did not avoid me for being different; rather, she cherished me.
When she was scolded by our mother for something ordinary and I approached our mother to ask "Why are you angry?", my question often brought an end to the lecture.
My sister would then always say "Thank you," possibly thinking that I had taken her side.
Having little interest in sweets or toys myself, I often gave them to her.
As a result, she was always following me around.
"Dad loved yakitori, so let's roast this and eat it today," I repeated clearly, thinking she hadn't heard me the first time.
My mother looked shocked.
The other woman next to her also seemed startled as her eyes, nostrils and mouth all opened wide in surprise.
Her reaction seemed funny enough to make me laugh, but then I noticed her gaze focused on my hand and thought that one bird wouldn't be enough.
"Should we catch more?"
As my eyes casually turned towards several sparrows nearby walking side by side, finally coming out of their shock my mother shouted "Keiko!" in a reproving tone of voice.
"Let's bury the small bird and make a grave for it.
Look everyone is crying now because they are sad their friend died; isn't it pitiful?"
"Why?
It already died anyway.
At my query, Mother was at a loss for words.
I quickly bagged the canned coffee, cigarettes, and hot dog in a small plastic bag.
Meanwhile, the man who had been jingling coins in his pocket suddenly stuck his hand into his chest pocket.
From this gesture, I immediately inferred that he was going to pay with electronic money.
"Welcome, good morning!"
Nodding slightly in acknowledgment, I accept the canned coffee handed to me by a male customer.
"Ah, and a pack of number 5 cigarettes as well.
"Understood.
I quickly pull out the Marlboro Light Menthol and scan it at the register.
"I'll need you to confirm your age on screen.
As he touches the screen, his gaze shifts slowly over to a showcase filled with fast food.
When I notice this change in his behavior, I halt my movements.

"Would you like something else?" although it would be appropriate for me to ask him this question, when customers seem indecisive about what they want to buy next; my policy is rather step back and wait.
At the faint sound of change ringing, I turn and my gaze shifts to the register.
Most people who jingle coins in their palms or pockets intend to quickly buy cigarettes or a newspaper and then leave, so I make it a point to be attentive to such sounds.
Sure enough, there was a man nearby who had a canned coffee in one hand while the other was thrust into his pocket as he approached the register.
With agility, I move around inside the shop and position myself behind the counter so as not to keep this customer waiting.
A convenience store is filled with sounds.
The chime of entering customers, the voice of an idol advertising new products through in-store radio broadcasts.
The shouts of employees, the sound of scanning barcodes.
The sound of items being put in baskets, bags of bread being grabbed, and the noise from heels walking around inside the store.
Everything mixes together to form "the sounds of a convenience store," constantly resonating in my eardrums.
